fields.apa_citation: Bourikas, L., Gauthier, S., Khor Song En, N., & Xiong, P. (2021). Effect of thermal, acoustic and air quality perception interactions on the comfort and satisfaction of people in office buildings. Energies, 14(2), 333. https://doi.org/10.3390/en14020333
fields.main_conclusion: In real office buildings, occupants' thermal sensation is associated with both their air-quality perception and their noise perception, and although the two-way interaction between air quality and noise did not significantly affect thermal sensation, operative temperature and sound pressure level each interact significantly with air-quality perception, making air-quality perception a key, previously under-recognized driver of occupant comfort and satisfaction.
independent_variables: Interaction terms (ASV x NSV; Top x ASV; SPL30 x ASV)
dependent_variables: Thermal preference vote (TPV) / thermal comfort vote (TCV)
fields.construct_pair: Air quality and noise perception (with operative temperature and sound pressure level) -> Thermal sensation/comfort
fields.stimulus_description: No experimentally manipulated stimulus was presented; occupants in three real, mixed-mode university office buildings reported their momentary thermal, acoustic and air-quality perceptions via short 'right-here-right-now' surveys while going about normal work, and in one building (Stage 3) their office's sound pressure level, air temperature and relative humidity were concurrently logged.
fields.methods_surface_summary: A three-stage field study: Stage 1 was a Building Use Studies post-occupancy evaluation survey (n=26) in one building; Stage 2 was a year-long weekly comfort survey (1079 valid responses from 116 participants) in two other buildings assessing thermal, preference, noise and air-quality votes; Stage 3 was a 5-week focused comfort survey (52 valid responses from 12 participants) in the first building paired with continuous environmental monitoring. Associations were tested with Goodman-Kruskal's gamma, Kendall's tau-b correlation, and mixed-effects (logistic) regression with participant ID as a random effect.
measurement_inventory: 7-point noise/acoustic perception vote (NSV) and acoustic comfort vote (NSC)
Building Use Studies (BUS) satisfaction questionnaire (7-point scale)

notes.sample_n: The paper has three separate samples (Stage 1: n=26; Stage 2: 116 unique participants producing 1079 responses over 48 weeks; Stage 3: 12 participants producing 52 responses over 5 weeks). Stage 2 is the largest, longest-running survey directly testing the paper's central TSV~ASV+NSV hypothesis, so its 116 individual participants was taken as 'the main study' sample_n; the 1079-response count is the response-level (not person-level) n for that same stage.
notes.direction: Multiple, partly opposite-signed relationships are reported: TSV correlates negatively with ASV (G=-0.114) but positively with NSV (G=+0.109 as printed, though the surrounding text's sign convention is inconsistent/possibly a typo); the ASV x NSV interaction on TSV is non-significant; the Top x ASV and SPL30 x ASV interactions are both significant but opposite in sign (-0.408 to -0.051 vs. +0.117 to +0.491 in Table 7). Coded 'mixed' because no single consistent direction summarizes the IV-DV relations.
notes.p_value: p=0.026 is the Goodman-Kruskal's gamma test p-value for the TSV~ASV association (Stage 2), chosen as representative of the paper's central 'thermal sensation is associated with air quality perception' claim; the final mixed-effects model's interaction terms are reported only via 95% confidence intervals (Table 7), not printed p-values, though text states these effects were significant at p<0.05.
notes.effect_size: G=-0.114 (Goodman-Kruskal's gamma) is the effect size printed for the TSV~ASV correlation referenced above; the final regression model's standardized coefficients are given as confidence intervals (Table 7) rather than point effect sizes with p-values, so a single 'main finding' effect size beyond this correlation is not unambiguous.
